podcast.body: This album was a groundbreaking milestone, becoming the first-ever rap record to top the charts and demonstrate that rap and hip hop were enduring genres capable of coexisting with rock music. It served as many white kids' initial exposure to this new, combined sound of rock, hip hop, and rap, and is cited as an inspiration for numerous bands like Korn, Limp Bizkit, and Linkin Park. The album entered the top 40 on December 20, 1986, staying for over nine months, and eventually hit number one in early 1987, where it remained for seven consecutive weeks. "License to ill was the first ever number one hip hop record."

podcast.title: Chart-Topping Debut
podcast.body: Released on November 15, 1986, this album was a monumental success, becoming the first rap album ever to top the charts. It combined punk, rock, rap, funk, and hip hop into a globally successful formula and featured Kerry King of Slayer on guitar, introducing countless millions, especially white suburban kids, to hip hop. "And of course, things completely exploded with their license to Il Album which came out on November 15th in 1986."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Parody of Hip Hop
podcast.body: The debut album was initially perceived as a parody of hip hop, leading to the band being pigeonholed as a novelty act for the first eight years of their career. Despite its humorous nature, Rolling Stone magazine acknowledged its significant impact. Profits from this album were later used to fund their G-Sun studio. "License to ill was a parody of hip hop. It was a good one, but it was still a parody."

podcast.title: Annual Sales
podcast.body: In previous decades, the Beastie Boys' album *License to Ill* consistently sold 2 million copies every year. "The Beastie boys used to sell 2 million copies of license to ill every year."
